nameStory: This goldenrod gets its 'wrinkle-leaved' name from its distinctively textured foliage that looks like it's been crumpled up and smoothed out again. The scientific name 'rugosa' comes from the Latin word for wrinkled or rough, perfectly describing those characteristic bumpy, veined leaves that feel like fine sandpaper.
description: Common wrinkle-leaved goldenrod is a sturdy perennial wildflower that brightens New England's late summer landscape with its cheerful yellow blooms. Growing 2-5 feet tall, this native plant produces arching sprays of tiny golden flowers arranged in graceful, one-sided clusters. Its rough-textured stems and distinctively wrinkled leaves make it one of the easier goldenrods to identify among New England's many yellow-flowered species. Like other goldenrods, it's a member of the sunflower family, with each 'flower' actually being a cluster of many tiny individual blooms.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel distinctly rough and bumpy to the touch, like fine sandpaper, with pronounced veining that creates a wrinkled appearance. They're oval-shaped with toothed edges and grow alternately up the stem.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower clusters arch outward in graceful, one-sided sprays that curve like tiny golden waterfalls. Each spray contains dozens of small composite flowers that bloom from late summer into fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 2-5 feet tall with multiple branching stems that often lean slightly outward. The plant spreads by underground runners to form colonies over time.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems feel rough and hairy to the touch, often with a slightly reddish tinge. They're sturdy but flexible, bending rather than breaking in wind.

habitat: Look for wrinkle-leaved goldenrod in moist to moderately wet areas like meadows, stream banks, woodland edges, and roadside ditches. It thrives in partial shade to full sun and tolerates a variety of soil types, from clay to loam, as long as there's adequate moisture. You'll often find it growing alongside asters, Joe Pye weed, and other late-season wildflowers in New England's wetland margins.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as fuzzy, reddish stems with small wrinkled leaves beginning to unfurl from the base.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height with distinctive rough-textured leaves clearly visible, but flowers haven't yet appeared until late in the season.
seasonality.fall: Spectacular golden flower displays peak in September and October, followed by fluffy white seed heads that catch the autumn light.
seasonality.winter: Dried brown stems and seed heads persist through snow, providing food for birds and helping identify locations for next year's growth.

funFact: Despite the common belief that goldenrod causes hay fever, it's actually innocent! The real culprit is ragweed, which blooms at the same time but has inconspicuous green flowers. Goldenrod's heavy, sticky pollen is designed for bees and butterflies, not wind dispersal, so it rarely becomes airborne enough to trigger allergies.
confusionNotes: With 26 goldenrod species in New England, identification can be tricky! The key to wrinkle-leaved goldenrod is right in the name - run your fingers over the leaves and feel for that distinctive sandpaper texture. Most other goldenrods have smooth or only slightly rough leaves, making this tactile test a reliable field identifier.
contextualKnowledge: Goldenrods suffered from unfortunate timing and poor public relations - blooming exactly when ragweed releases its allergy-causing pollen into the air. This coincidence led to decades of wrongful blame for hay fever symptoms, causing many people to avoid these beautiful and ecologically important native plants.
compareHints: Among New England's goldenrods, wrinkle-leaved goldenrod stands out for its distinctly rough, sandpapery leaves - most others like Canada goldenrod or giant goldenrod have smooth foliage. Its flower clusters also arch more gracefully in one-sided sprays compared to the more upright, plume-like arrangements of tall goldenrod or the flat-topped clusters of field goldenrod.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's 25+ goldenrod species, seaside goldenrod stands out with its thick, fleshy leaves and coastal habitat - most other goldenrods have thin, papery leaves and prefer inland locations.
Among its 25+ goldenrod cousins in New England, silverrod is unmistakable due to its white flowers.
Among the 26 goldenrod species in New England, bluestem is unique for its blue-purple stem and woodland habitat preference.
Among the 25+ goldenrod species in New England, broad-leaved goldenrod is unique in its woodland habitat and zigzag stem.
Among New England's many goldenrods, early goldenrod stands out for its July bloom time and graceful, arching flower plumes.
Among New England's many goldenrods, Canada goldenrod is distinguished by its gracefully arching, plume-like flower clusters and smooth stems.
Among New England's many goldenrods, field goldenrod stands out for being one of the shortest and grayest.
Among New England's many goldenrods, giant goldenrod stands out for its impressive height — it's typically the tallest species you'll encounter.
Among New England's many goldenrods, downy goldenrod is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture on both stems and leaves.
Cutler's goldenrod is much shorter and more compact than common lowland species like Canada goldenrod or tall goldenrod, which can reach 6 feet or more.
Among New England goldenrods, large-leaved stands out immediately for its broad foliage — most others like Canada goldenrod and field goldenrod have much narrower, more lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's goldenrods, tall goldenrod stands out for its impressive height and pyramid-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's many goldenrods, sweet goldenrod is the only one with that distinctive anise fragrance - this makes it the easiest goldenrod to identify with certainty.
Among New England's many goldenrods, bog goldenrod stands out for its wetland habitat requirement and impressive height.
Among New England's many goldenrods, squarrose goldenrod stands out for its exceptionally narrow, elongated flower cluster that stays tightly upright rather than spreading outward.
Among New England's 26 goldenrod species, swamp goldenrod is unique for its wetland habitat - no other goldenrod in our region specifically seeks out waterlogged soils.

Among New England's many goldenrods, cut-leaf goldenrod stands out for its preference for woodland settings rather than open fields, and its more delicate, open flower arrangement compared to the dense, plume-like clusters of field-loving species like Canada goldenrod.
Among New England's goldenrods, Elliott's stands out for its exceptional height and strict coastal marsh habitat - most other goldenrods prefer drier upland sites.
Among New England's many goldenrods, showy goldenrod stands out for its impressive height and dense, pyramid-shaped flower clusters.

Among New England's many goldenrods, hairy goldenrod stands out for its distinctly rough, bristly texture - much more pronounced than the slight fuzziness of Canada goldenrod or the smooth stems of giant goldenrod.

Among New England's many goldenrods, stiff-leaved goldenrod stands out for its flat-topped flower clusters (versus the branching plumes of Canada goldenrod or tall goldenrod) and especially its thick, rigid leaves that feel completely different from the soft, flexible foliage of common species.
Unlike its yellow-flowered goldenrod cousins that typically have branching, plume-like flower clusters, white flat-topped goldenrod has distinctively flat, white flower heads.
Unlike the abundant Canada Goldenrod or Giant Goldenrod with their large, spreading flower clusters, Sticky Goldenrod has more compact, narrow flower heads.
Among New England goldenrods, elm-leaved goldenrod is unique for its broad, elm-like leaves - most others like Canada goldenrod and tall goldenrod have narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's many goldenrods, racemose goldenrod is unique for its simple, unbranched flower spike - all other regional goldenrods have branching flower clusters.
Rand's goldenrod differs from common goldenrods by its specialized rocky mountain habitat and extreme rarity.
